Data: [TidyTuesday 2026-09-08](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2026/2026-09-08).

The cappuccino index asks a good question: how long does the person who makes the coffee have to work to buy it?
The answer arrives as a table of 87 countries, each with a time in minutes and seconds, sorted fastest first.
It reads like a leaderboard.
For most of its length it is not one.

Twenty-five of the 87 countries were surveyed at exactly one café.
Forty-one were surveyed at fewer than five.
One café is enough to compute a ratio, and the ratio can be printed to the second, but it cannot say what the country does.
Qatar sits at 186:59 on a single café.
The figure leaves all 41 out, because a country with one café has no interval to draw, and drawing the number alone would repeat the table's mistake.

Where there are enough cafés, the interval is worth having, and it changes the reading of the top of the table.
Australia is genuinely first: 10:04 on 171 cafés, and its interval spans 9:48 to 10:20.
Italy is second at 11:51, on 15 cafés, and its interval runs from 9:09 to 14:34.
That reaches below Australia's index and past the fourth-placed country.
Second place is not a fact about Italy, it is a fact about fifteen cafés.

The clock is the unit of the index, so the figure uses it.
One turn of the cup is an hour.
Australia sits a sixth of the way round the first turn, the United Kingdom and France a little further on, and India is still going on the third turn at 172:10.
Reading the spiral inwards is reading the working day get longer.
Pakistan is further out still, at 277:02, and is one of the countries the figure does not draw: two cafés.

Three cautions.
The interval covers the sampling of cafés and nothing else.
It says nothing about which cities were visited, and the survey is not a random sample of anywhere: it is what people sent in.
A wide interval here means few cafés, and a narrow one means many, not that the number is right.

Second, the index is a ratio of sums, not an average of ratios.
It answers what the country's total coffee costs against the country's total wages, so the busiest, most expensive cities pull it more than a per-café average would.
Within Mexico, the middle 80% of cafés run from 40 to 117 minutes, a spread of nearly three to one, and one national number cannot hold that.

Third, tips are excluded throughout, which matters most in the countries where tips are most of the wage.
